title: Migrating JavaScript to TypeScript
summary: Migrating a JS codebase to TypeScript is an *incremental* process: enable `allowJs`, rename files to `.ts` gradually, ratchet up strictness in degrees, contain `any` deliberately, and use `// @ts-check` + JSDoc to type JS before converting it.

subtopics.title: Incremental migration with allowJs
subtopics.explanation: allowJs lets TypeScript compile and type-aware-check .js files alongside .ts, so you can introduce TypeScript without converting everything at once. Pair it with checkJs (or per-file // @ts-check) to start surfacing type errors in existing JS. This keeps the app building the entire time.

subtopics.title: Renaming files to .ts gradually
subtopics.explanation: Convert file-by-file, usually starting at the leaves of the dependency graph (utilities with few dependencies) and working up. Renaming .js to .ts turns on full checking for that file; fix its errors, then move to the next. Avoid a big-bang rename — it produces an unreviewable error avalanche.

subtopics.title: Strict-by-degrees
subtopics.explanation: Don't enable strict: true on day one. Turn on individual flags progressively — start with noImplicitAny off, get the project compiling, then enable noImplicitAny, then strictNullChecks, etc., fixing fallout at each step. Each flag is a separate, reviewable migration milestone.
subtopics.example: // step 1: { strictNullChecks: false }  -> later: { strictNullChecks: true }

subtopics.title: Containing any during migration
subtopics.explanation: any is a legitimate temporary tool while migrating, but it must be contained: prefer unknown where you can, isolate any to file/module boundaries, and mark debts with // TODO or a custom type alias (type TODO = any) you can grep and remove later. Never let any silently spread through inference.
subtopics.example: type AnyForNow = any; // grep-able debt marker

subtopics.title: // @ts-check and JSDoc
subtopics.explanation: You can type JavaScript before converting it: add // @ts-check at the top of a .js file to enable checking, and describe types with JSDoc (@param, @returns, @typedef). This delivers much of TypeScript's safety in plain JS and de-risks the eventual rename.

subtopics.title: Tooling and escape hatches
subtopics.explanation: Use ts-migrate or codemods to auto-add annotations, // @ts-expect-error to mark and track known errors (it errors if the line later type-checks, so debt self-cleans), and tsc --noEmit in CI as the gate. Editors and ESLint (@typescript-eslint) catch issues continuously.

subtopics.title: Common pitfalls
subtopics.explanation: Pitfalls include a big-bang rename, enabling strict everywhere at once, overusing // @ts-ignore (which hides future real errors — prefer @ts-expect-error), letting any leak through inference, and skipping types for third-party libs. Treat migration as many small, green commits, not one heroic PR.

foundations.overview: Migrating JavaScript to TypeScript is best done incrementally rather than as a rewrite. TypeScript is designed for this: allowJs lets both languages coexist, files are renamed to .ts one at a time, and strictness is increased flag-by-flag. JSDoc plus // @ts-check let you gain type safety in plain JS before converting, and contained any provides a temporary escape hatch while the codebase ratchets toward full strictness.
foundations.formalDefinition: Incremental migration is the process of adopting TypeScript on an existing JavaScript project by (1) enabling JS/TS interop via allowJs, (2) converting files to .ts progressively, and (3) tightening compilerOptions strictness in stages, keeping the project compiling and shippable at every step.
foundations.whyItMatters: Most real TypeScript adoption happens on existing JavaScript, not greenfield. Knowing how to migrate without freezing feature work or breaking the build is a senior-level skill and a common interview/system-design topic, because a botched migration can stall a team for months.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of migration as a dimmer switch, not a light switch: you gradually increase type coverage and strictness, keeping the lights on (the app building and shipping) the whole time, instead of flipping everything to strict at once and plunging into an error avalanche.
foundations.browserPerspective: Migration is purely build-time; the shipped JavaScript is unaffected by how it was authored. allowJs and renames change what the compiler checks and emits, but the browser runs the same emitted JS — so users see no change while internal safety rises.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Teams enable allowJs, add // @ts-check + JSDoc to critical modules, convert leaf utilities to .ts first, enable noImplicitAny then strictNullChecks over successive sprints, and use // @ts-expect-error plus tsc --noEmit in CI to track and prevent regressions.
foundations.businessImpact: Incremental migration lets a team capture TypeScript's bug-prevention benefits without halting feature delivery, avoiding the cost and risk of a freeze-and-rewrite. Each strictness milestone reduces a class of production defects.
foundations.engineeringImpact: A staged plan keeps PRs small and reviewable, distributes the work, and prevents the morale-crushing 'thousands of errors at once' scenario. Contained any and grep-able debt markers keep technical debt visible and removable.
foundations.performanceImpact: No runtime impact on the shipped app. Build/check times rise as more files are checked; allowJs and incremental compilation help, and skipLibCheck avoids re-checking third-party declarations during the transition.
commonUseCases: Adopting TypeScript on a large existing JS app without a rewrite
Typing JS with // @ts-check + JSDoc before converting files
Tracking migration debt with // @ts-expect-error and type aliases for any

commonMisconceptions.myth: You must rewrite the whole codebase to start using TypeScript.
commonMisconceptions.reality: allowJs lets .js and .ts coexist, so you migrate file-by-file while the app keeps building and shipping.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Turn on strict: true immediately for maximum benefit.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Enabling all strict flags at once on legacy code produces an unmanageable error flood; enable them in stages.
@ts-expect-error errors if the line later compiles cleanly, so the suppression self-cleans; @ts-ignore silently hides future real errors too.

config.intro: Each step keeps the project green (building and shipping) before the next.

steps.name: Enable interop
steps.detail: Add a tsconfig with allowJs:true so .js and .ts compile together; the app still builds unchanged.

steps.name: Check JS in place
steps.detail: Add // @ts-check + JSDoc to key files (or checkJs) to surface type issues before any rename.

steps.name: Convert leaves first
steps.detail: Rename low-dependency utility files to .ts, fix their errors, and commit each conversion.

steps.name: Contain any
steps.detail: Use temporary, grep-able any (or unknown) at boundaries so inference stays controlled while you work upward.

steps.name: Ratchet strictness
steps.detail: Turn on noImplicitAny, then strictNullChecks, then the rest — one reviewable milestone at a time.

steps.name: Lock it in CI
steps.detail: Run tsc --noEmit in CI and remove debt markers until strict:true passes with no suppressions.

interactiveExamples.title: Typing JS with JSDoc + @ts-check
interactiveExamples.explanation: JSDoc gives plain JavaScript real type-checking under // @ts-check before any rename. The sandbox runs the JS; in an editor the wrong call would be flagged.

interactiveExamples.title: Containing any with a grep-able marker
interactiveExamples.explanation: A named alias for any makes migration debt searchable and removable later. The sandbox runs the logic; the alias is what keeps the debt visible.

codeLab.title: Convert a JS helper to typed TS
codeLab.instructions: Take this untyped JS helper and convert it as you would during migration: add explicit parameter and return types and remove the implicit any. Keep behavior identical.
hints: Type the parameter as string[] and annotate the return type.
Give the accumulator an explicit type like Record<string, string[]> to avoid implicit any.

debuggingLab.title: @ts-ignore hides a real new bug
debuggingLab.symptom: A line was suppressed with // @ts-ignore during migration; later the code changed and introduced a genuine type error that stays hidden.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: // @ts-ignore suppresses ALL errors on the next line, forever. The later typo timeoot produces undefined, but the suppression hides it. @ts-expect-error is safer: it requires an error to exist and reports if the line ever type-checks cleanly, so stale suppressions surface.
commonMistakes: Reaching for // @ts-ignore as the default suppression.
Leaving suppressions in place after the underlying error is fixed.
Suppressing instead of fixing or narrowing the type.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Remove the blanket ignore, fix the typo, and use @ts-expect-error only when a known error must be tracked.

theory.question: How do you migrate a large JavaScript codebase to TypeScript without halting feature work?
theory.directAnswer: Do it incrementally: add a tsconfig with allowJs so .js and .ts compile together, optionally check existing JS with // @ts-check and JSDoc, then convert files to .ts one at a time starting from leaf utilities. Tighten strictness flag-by-flag (noImplicitAny, then strictNullChecks, etc.), contain any deliberately, and gate everything with tsc --noEmit in CI so the app stays green and shippable throughout.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A staged adoption process that keeps the project compiling at every step.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A big-bang rewrite or enabling full strict at once produces an unmanageable error flood and stalls delivery.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: allowJs enables coexistence; per-file renames turn on full checking; progressive strict flags and CI gates ratchet safety up gradually.

theory.whyImportant: Most TS adoption is on existing JS; doing it without a freeze is what makes migration feasible for real teams.
theory.realWorldExample: A team enables allowJs, JSDoc-types its payment module, converts utils to .ts, then turns on strictNullChecks the following sprint.

nestedTopics.title: Leaf-first order
nestedTopics.explanation: Convert low-dependency files first to limit cascading errors.

nestedTopics.title: CI gate
nestedTopics.explanation: tsc --noEmit prevents regressions as files convert.

followUps.question: Why not just enable strict immediately?
followUps.answer: On legacy code it surfaces thousands of errors at once, which is unreviewable and blocks shipping; staging keeps each step small and green.

theory.question: How do // @ts-check, JSDoc, // @ts-ignore, and // @ts-expect-error fit into a migration?
theory.directAnswer: // @ts-check turns on type-checking for a .js file, and JSDoc (@param/@returns/@typedef) supplies the types — together giving safety before any rename. For unavoidable errors during migration, // @ts-expect-error is preferred over // @ts-ignore because @ts-expect-error requires an error to be present and flags the line if it ever becomes valid, so suppressions self-clean; @ts-ignore hides errors silently and forever.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A set of comment directives plus JSDoc for typing and selectively suppressing in JS/TS.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To type plain JS pre-conversion and to track unavoidable errors without abandoning checking.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: @ts-check enables the checker per file; JSDoc annotations feed it types; the expect-error directive ties a suppression to an actual error so it can be detected when stale.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing expect-error over ignore keeps suppressions honest and prevents new bugs from hiding behind old waivers.
theory.realWorldExample: A legacy file gets // @ts-check + JSDoc to find bugs first; one stubborn call is marked // @ts-expect-error with a TODO to revisit.

nestedTopics.title: @typedef
nestedTopics.explanation: JSDoc can define reusable object/types for JS files.

nestedTopics.title: Self-cleaning waivers
nestedTopics.explanation: @ts-expect-error errors once the underlying issue is fixed, prompting removal.

followUps.question: When is @ts-ignore acceptable?
followUps.answer: Rarely — when an error genuinely can't be expressed (e.g. a known compiler quirk) and even then it should carry a comment and be revisited; default to @ts-expect-error.

scenario.question: Your team flipped strict: true across a 200k-line JS-to-TS conversion and now there are ~3,000 errors blocking all merges. How do you recover?
scenario.directAnswer: Back off the big-bang: revert to strict: false and re-enable flags individually, starting with the cheapest wins (noImplicitAny) and tackling strictNullChecks last since it's the largest. Get the build green immediately by temporarily relaxing the flags, then drive each flag to zero errors in dedicated, reviewable PRs. Track remaining suppressions with // @ts-expect-error and a grep-able any alias, and add tsc --noEmit to CI so no new errors creep in while you burn down the backlog.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A recovery plan that converts one unmanageable error flood into staged, mergeable work.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Enabling all strict flags at once on legacy code overwhelms review and blocks delivery.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Per-flag rollout plus CI gating and debt markers turns 3,000 errors into a series of bounded, green milestones.

scenario.whyImportant: This is the classic real-world migration failure mode; the fix demonstrates pragmatic strictness sequencing.

nestedTopics.title: Flag sequencing
nestedTopics.explanation: noImplicitAny is usually cheaper to satisfy than strictNullChecks.

nestedTopics.title: Burn-down tracking
nestedTopics.explanation: Grep-able markers quantify remaining debt per flag.

followUps.question: How do you stop new files from regressing?
followUps.answer: Gate CI with tsc --noEmit and lint rules so new code must satisfy the strict flags even while legacy debt is being burned down.

coding.question: Convert this untyped JS function to strict-safe TypeScript: it takes a config object that may omit fields and returns a normalized result. Handle the optional/undefined cases that strictNullChecks would flag.
coding.thoughtProcess: Under strictNullChecks, optional fields are T | undefined and must be defaulted before use. I'll define an input interface with optional members and an output interface with required members, then apply defaults via nullish coalescing so the return type has no undefined. This mirrors the real work of satisfying strict during migration.
coding.lineByLine: RawConfig marks every field optional (the legacy reality); Config requires them (the normalized contract). normalizeConfig defaults a missing raw to {} and uses ?? to substitute defaults only when a value is null/undefined, so the returned Config has no undefined fields — satisfying strictNullChecks.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) — a fixed number of fields.

alternativeApproaches.title: Object spread with defaults
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Spread a defaults object then the raw, but ?? per-field avoids letting an explicit undefined override a default.
alternativeApproaches.code: // return { ...defaults, ...raw } // careful: an explicit undefined in raw overrides

followUps.question: Why ?? instead of ||?
followUps.answer: || treats 0 and '' as falsy and would wrongly replace valid values like timeout 0; ?? only substitutes for null/undefined.

systemDesign.question: Design a migration plan and tooling/CI strategy to move a large multi-team JavaScript monorepo to strict TypeScript over two quarters without freezing feature development.
systemDesign.directAnswer: Stage it as a program, not a PR. Phase 0: add a base tsconfig with allowJs and strict:false, get the monorepo compiling, and add tsc --noEmit to CI per package. Phase 1: enforce that all new files are .ts and that JS files carry // @ts-check + JSDoc (lint-enforced), so the bleeding stops. Phase 2: convert package-by-package leaf-first, owned by the responsible team, tracking coverage with a dashboard (percent .ts, count of any/@ts-expect-error). Phase 3: ratchet strict flags one at a time across packages (noImplicitAny first, strictNullChecks last), each as its own milestone, with a CI ratchet that forbids increasing error/suppression counts. Use codemods/ts-migrate for bulk annotation, contain any behind a grep-able alias, and prefer @ts-expect-error so suppressions self-clean. Define ownership, a tracking metric, and a non-regression gate as the backbone.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A phased, multi-team migration architecture with CI ratchets and per-package ownership.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Coordinating many teams and packages requires preventing regressions and distributing work without a freeze.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: allowJs + per-package tsconfig enables coexistence; CI ratchets cap debt; leaf-first per-package conversion and staged strict flags advance coverage measurably.

systemDesign.whyImportant: Org-scale migrations fail without ownership, metrics, and non-regression gates; this is exactly what senior/staff interviews probe.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: Large products (e.g. Airbnb-, Stripe-style frontends) migrated by enforcing TS for new code, converting incrementally, and ratcheting strictness with CI gates over multiple quarters.

nestedTopics.title: CI ratchet
nestedTopics.explanation: A gate that fails if the count of errors/suppressions rises, ensuring monotonic progress.

nestedTopics.title: Per-package tsconfig
nestedTopics.explanation: Project references and per-package settings let packages migrate at different speeds.

nestedTopics.title: Coverage dashboard
nestedTopics.explanation: Track percent typed and remaining any to show momentum and target hotspots.

followUps.question: How do you keep teams from stalling on the hardest package?
followUps.answer: Assign explicit ownership, allow per-package strictness so the rest of the repo advances independently, and budget dedicated time for high-debt packages rather than blocking the whole program on them.

followUps.question: What metric signals success?
followUps.answer: Percent of files as strict .ts with zero @ts-ignore/@ts-expect-error and a fully passing strict tsc --noEmit across all packages.

productionDeepDive.architecture: A migration is structured in phases: interop (allowJs), stop-the-bleeding (TS-only for new code, JSDoc for legacy), conversion (leaf-first, per-package ownership), and strictness ratchet (flags one at a time). In a monorepo, per-package tsconfig and project references let packages migrate at independent speeds.
productionDeepDive.performance: No runtime effect on shipped code; build/check time grows as coverage rises. allowJs, incremental builds, project references, and skipLibCheck keep type-check times manageable during the transition.
productionDeepDive.security: Strictness gains (especially strictNullChecks) remove undefined-dereference and unchecked-data bugs that can become vulnerabilities. While migrating, contained any at boundaries should be paired with runtime validation so untyped data isn't blindly trusted.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Org-scale migrations need ownership, a coverage metric, and a CI ratchet that forbids increasing error/suppression counts, so progress is monotonic across many teams and packages instead of regressing.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Grep-able any markers, @ts-expect-error (not @ts-ignore), and per-flag milestones keep debt visible and self-cleaning. Lint rules (@typescript-eslint) enforce TS-for-new-code and ban silent suppressions.
productionDeepDive.observability: tsc --noEmit in CI is the gate; a dashboard tracking percent .ts, any count, and suppression count makes progress measurable; @ts-expect-error surfaces stale suppressions automatically.

caseStudies.problem: Big JS codebases needed type safety but couldn't freeze feature work for a rewrite.
caseStudies.solution: Incremental adoption: allowJs, TS-for-new-code policy, leaf-first conversion, and staged strict flags with CI ratchets.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Longer total timeline and interim any debt, but continuous shipping and no morale-crushing error floods.
caseStudies.lessons: Migration succeeds as a measured, owned, non-regressing program — not a heroic single rewrite.

keyTakeaways: Migrate incrementally: allowJs lets .js and .ts coexist so you convert file-by-file while shipping.
